title: Five Ways To Use Self-Explanation Prompts
author: Blanksby, Alex
summary: Alex Blanksby extends his Five Ways series to self-explanation prompts, opening with Willingham's "memory is the residue of thought" to argue that if we want students to remember the reasoning behind a worked example, we have to prompt them to explain and elaborate on it rather than assuming that reading alone gets the job done. He details concrete "why" and "what if" question stems from Pershan's work for prompting self-explanation, and separately covers how to teach students to give better explanations in the first place, using sentence stems and scaffolded fill-in-the-blank explanations that gradually withdraw support. He draws on Watson and Mason's catalogue of general prompting questions as reusable tools, cautioning against trying to memorise the whole list at once. His fourth section, on constraints, is the most theoretically dense: citing Rittle-Johnson and Loehr, he warns that self-explanation works better on content known to be correct or incorrect than on students' own tentative ideas, since explaining a flawed personal idea can entrench it rather than correct it, and that badly designed prompts can inadvertently redirect attention away from other important information. He closes with a practical caution, "pick your battles," noting that constant demands for explanation are exhausting for both student and teacher and should be reserved for moments when the payoff justifies the cost.
points: Blanksby's grounding claim, borrowed from Willingham, is that "memory is the residue of thought": students remember what they're prompted to think about, which is the whole justification for self-explanation prompts existing at all.

His constraint from Rittle-Johnson and Loehr is a genuine caution against a popular idea: self-explaining one's own possibly wrong reasoning can entrench errors rather than fix them, unlike explaining known-correct or known-incorrect worked material.
His "pick your battles" closing section explicitly names the tradeoff between rich explanation and lesson pace, rather than presenting self-explanation as costless good practice.
The sentence-stem and fill-in-the-blank scaffolds give a concrete, gradually-withdrawn structure for teaching explanation quality itself, not just prompting for it.
quotes: If "memory is the residue of thought", that is, we remember the aspect(s) of something that we think about, how do we ensure students are thinking about the things that will help them learn? (Willingham, 2009).

More successful self-explainers tend to relate a step in a worked solution or feature of an object to an underlying principle, whereas less successful self-explainers tend to give superficial explanations often due to studying the examples for very little time.

[S]elf-explanation is often more effective when learners are explaining content that they know is correct or incorrect rather than their own ideas." Whatever students explain is more likely to stay in their memory.

[E]xplanation prompts must be designed with care so that efforts to direct attention towards one type of information does not come at the expense of learning less about another important type of information.

A student can't explain what they don't know. Asking for an explanation when the student does not have the necessary prior knowledge (activated or at all) will devolve the process into playing the terrible "guess what's in my head" game.
